deep.reconstruction:
Page headed 'Litt: B'. It is a table of biquadratic (fourth-power) residues for primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4), with p from 5 to 293 (277, 281, 293 run into the margin and the next page). It continues the work on the previous page: Gaussian 4-periods, Π^0 = -1/4 + (1/4)√p + (1/2)p^{1/4} cos(φ/2) with p = a²+4b². It feeds the next page: the criterion 'Zu 1 gehört a+ib wenn (a+ib)^{(p±1)/4} = a±ib' and tables of the biquadratic character of -1, ±2, -3, 5, -7, -11, 13, 17 in terms of a and b.

Column 2 (in brackets for the first five rows) gives a.b with p = a² + 4b², a odd. Examples: 5 = 1+4·1; 13 = 9+4; 41 = 25+4·4; 137 = 121+4·4; 257 = 1+4·64; 293 = 289+4. All 30 entries are correct.

Column 3 gives the biquadratic residues B = {x : x^{(p-1)/4} ≡ 1 mod p}, of which there are (p-1)/4. The notation depends on p mod 8.

(i) p ≡ 1 (mod 8). Here -1 is a biquadratic residue, so B = -B. Gauss writes '±' followed by the (p-1)/8 elements of B in 1..(p-1)/2.
- p = 17: ±1, 4, i.e. {1, 4, 13, 16}.
- p = 73, 89, 113: the lists are exactly the orbits of 2 under doubling, reduced to ±. For 89: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64→25, 50→39, 78→11, 22, 44.

(ii) p ≡ 5 (mod 8). Here -1 is a quadratic but not a biquadratic residue. So for each quadratic residue x ≤ (p-1)/2, exactly one of ±x lies in B. Gauss writes +x or -x accordingly, giving (p-1)/4 signed entries. I checked these by hand:
- p = 13: +1+3-4, from B = {1, 3, 9}.
- p = 29: +1-4-5-6+7-9-13, from B = {1, 7, 16, 20, 23, 24, 25}.
- p = 37: +1-3-4+7+9+10-11+12+16, from B = {1, 7, 9, 10, 12, 16, 26, 33, 34}.
- p = 53 and p = 61: checked entry by entry, writing x = y² and testing whether y is a quadratic residue.

Implicit pattern (my observation): 2 appears in the ± lists exactly for p = 73, 89, 113, 233, 257, 281. These are the primes of the form a² + 64y². This agrees with Gauss's later theorem that 2 is a biquadratic residue iff b ≡ 0 (mod 8) in p = a² + b².

Entry counts agree with (p-1)/4 or (p-1)/8 for every row I counted (101, 109, 149, 157, 173, 181, 193, 197, and 269 including its continuation on the next page), except:
- 229 (56 entries instead of 57);
- 233 and 241 (one entry short in the legible text, among overwritten or blotted entries);
- 257 (heavily overwritten).
errors: p=137: the list ends '...64.65.74'. The correct representative ≤68 is 63. 74 ≡ -63 is a biquadratic residue, so this is a residue left unreduced: 28² ≡ 99 ≡ -38 and 38² = 1444 ≡ 74. My computed B for 137 is ±{1,4,14,15,16,18,22,34,38,49,50,56,59,60,63,64,65}.
p=229: only 56 of the required 57 signed entries appear. The quadratic residue 48 is missing between -46 and -49. This is apparently an omission by Gauss; the image shows '-45-46-49+51'.
p=233 and p=241: the legible lists contain 28 and 29 entries, but (p-1)/8 = 29 and 30 are required. Entries are lost or obscured among the deletions; this cannot be decided from the image.
p=61 and p=53: the blotted entries must be -5, -14 (for 61) and -17 (for 53). Computation confirms these signs; the blots hide the minus signs rather than marking errors.

results.what: Table of p = a² + 4b² representations for primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 up to 293
Complete lists of biquadratic residues mod p for p ≡ 1 mod 4 up to 293, in compact notation: ± lists for p ≡ 1 mod 8, signed quadratic-residue lists for p ≡ 5 mod 8
results.modern_name: Quartic residue tables / quartic residue character
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum, 1828/1832); Jacobi's Canon arithmeticus (1839)

results.what: Implicit data supporting 'the biquadratic character of 2 is determined by b mod 8 in p = a² + 4b²' (2 ∈ B iff p = x² + 64y²)

deep.surprise_reason: These are computational tables underlying Gauss's well-documented 1805-1807 investigations of biquadratic residues, published in outline in 1828. The page holds raw data, not new theory; only minor slips are notable.

checkable.asserts: Each listed prime has the form a²+4b² (pairs as in column 2)

Row 137: the uncertain '14[?]. 15[?]' are indeed 14 and 15 (confirmed by computation).

Row 257: the overwritten list very likely encodes 23, 34, 46, 67 (not 68 alone) and 92, giving the correct 32 entries (the computed list has both 67 and 68); the items read as 95[?], 121[?] are 95 and 121.
